title: A Systematic Review of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring and Optimal Sensor Placement

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement
subsections.subsection_title: Structural Health Monitoring Objectives and Lifecycle
subsections.content:
Structural health monitoring (SHM) seeks to infer the condition of a structure from measured responses so that safety, serviceability, and maintenance decisions can be made on a rational basis. Early formulations emphasized continuous or periodic observation to detect abnormal changes, but later work clarified that SHM spans a hierarchy of objectives ranging from damage detection and localization to severity assessment, prognosis, and decision support ref [1], ref [2]. In this sense, sensing is not an end in itself: it is the information backbone for model validation, uncertainty reduction, and risk-informed asset management across the life of civil, aerospace, and mechanical systems ref [3], ref [4].

A useful lifecycle view distinguishes baseline characterization during design and commissioning, operational monitoring during service, event-triggered assessment after hazards, and long-term updating of digital or physics-based models. Farrar and Worden framed this progression through the widely adopted four-level damage identification paradigm, while Sohn et al. and Worden and Farrar linked SHM to statistical pattern recognition, highlighting the need to separate environmental and operational variability from genuine damage-sensitive features ref [2], ref [5], ref [6]. For large infrastructure, this lifecycle perspective also connects monitoring to inspection planning and performance management, as illustrated in bridge and infrastructure SHM reviews ref [7], ref [8].

These objectives directly shape sensor placement. If the goal is model updating, sensors should maximize identifiability of modal or state parameters; if the goal is damage diagnosis or prognosis, placement should instead favor sensitivity to likely damage scenarios, robustness to noise, and practical maintainability over decades of operation ref [3], ref [4], ref [9]. Thus, optimal sensor placement is best understood as a lifecycle design problem in which sensing strategies must remain informative under changing structural states, environmental conditions, and decision requirements ref [1], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement
subsections.subsection_title: Types of Structures and Monitoring Scenarios
subsections.content:
Optimal sensor placement depends strongly on the class of structure being monitored, because structural topology, dominant loading, accessibility, and failure modes determine both what should be sensed and where sensors are most informative. Civil SHM has focused heavily on long-span bridges, where ambient and traffic-induced vibration, temperature variation, and local deterioration interact across large spatial scales; representative deployments include cable-stayed and suspension bridges such as the Tsing Ma Bridge and the Guangzhou New TV Tower, which illustrate the need for multi-type sensing over distributed geometries ref [10], ref [11]. Building structures, especially tall buildings and base-isolated systems, emphasize wind and seismic response, occupant safety, and post-event rapid assessment, motivating configurations tailored to modal identification and interstory drift estimation ref [7], ref [12].

A second major distinction concerns monitoring scenario. Some systems are designed for continuous in-service surveillance under operational and environmental variability, while others target periodic inspection, event-triggered recording during earthquakes or typhoons, or temporary campaigns for model validation. This distinction affects acceptable power consumption, data bandwidth, and redundancy, and therefore changes the sensor placement objective from persistent damage detectability to transient capture or diagnosis under sparse instrumentation ref [1], ref [13]. Offshore platforms and wind turbines add further complexity because hydrodynamic loading, rotating components, and difficult maintenance environments favor robust layouts with fault tolerance and remote communication capability ref [14], ref [15].

Monitoring goals also differ between new and aging infrastructure. For newly designed structures, sensor networks are often embedded to support digital twins, model calibration, and lifecycle management; for existing assets, placement must adapt to incomplete drawings, access limitations, and retrofitting constraints. Similar issues arise in aerospace composite structures, where guided-wave and strain-based sensing are often localized around damage-prone regions rather than distributed globally ref [16]. Consequently, structure type and operational scenario should be treated as first-order inputs to any sensor placement formulation rather than as secondary implementation details.

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement
subsections.content:
Sensor technologies in structural health monitoring span contact and non-contact modalities, each offering different trade-offs in spatial coverage, bandwidth, durability, and installation cost. Conventional point sensors such as strain gauges, accelerometers, displacement transducers, and piezoelectric transducers remain central because they provide high-fidelity local measurements for vibration-based identification, load estimation, and damage-sensitive feature extraction. Piezoelectric sensing, in particular, enables both passive and active interrogation through guided waves and electromechanical impedance, making it attractive for detecting small cracks and debonding in metallic and composite components ref [1], ref [17].

Optical and distributed sensing technologies have broadened SHM from sparse instrumentation toward dense and continuous field measurements. Fiber Bragg grating sensors support multiplexed strain and temperature measurements with electromagnetic immunity and have been widely studied for civil infrastructure and aerospace structures ref [18]. More generally, fiber-optic SHM systems can provide quasi-distributed or fully distributed measurements over long distances, which is valuable for pipelines, bridges, and large-area composites ref [19]. At the global scale, wireless sensor networks reduce cabling cost and enable scalable deployment, although power management, synchronization, and data loss become integral design constraints ref [20], ref [21].

Non-contact modalities further expand observability. Vision-based systems use cameras for displacement and vibration measurement, enabling rapid instrumentation of large structures ref [22], while laser Doppler vibrometry provides high-resolution vibration data without mass loading the structure ref [23]. Infrared thermography and acoustic emission complement dynamic sensing by targeting heat-flow anomalies and transient stress-wave events associated with cracking, delamination, and corrosion processes ref [24], ref [25]. Because each modality emphasizes different physical phenomena, optimal sensor placement must be understood jointly with sensing physics, feature extraction strategy, and the damage mechanisms of interest.

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement
subsections.subsection_title: Problem Definition of Optimal Sensor Placement
subsections.content:
Optimal sensor placement (OSP) in structural health monitoring is commonly formulated as the problem of selecting a subset of candidate sensing locations that maximizes information about structural states, parameters, or damage while satisfying resource constraints. In model-based settings, the decision variables are binary placement indicators, and the objective is often tied to estimation quality through the Fisher information matrix, modal observability, or prediction error covariance. Classical formulations include maximizing determinant- or trace-based criteria of the information matrix for parameter identification and dynamic state estimation, thereby linking OSP directly to identifiability and uncertainty reduction ref [26], ref [27], ref [28].

When the monitoring objective is modal testing or model updating, OSP is frequently posed to preserve linear independence of measured mode shapes or to maximize information entropy. Effective independence (EI) methods select locations that contribute most strongly to the rank and conditioning of the modal matrix, whereas entropy- and mutual-information-based formulations quantify redundancy and complementarity among sensors ref [29], ref [30], ref [31]. For damage detection, the objective may instead emphasize sensitivity to local stiffness loss, discrimination among damage scenarios, or robustness under modeling uncertainty, leading naturally to multiobjective and robust optimization formulations ref [32], ref [33].

Accordingly, the OSP problem is not a single canonical optimization task but a family of combinatorial designs defined by sensing modality, inference goal, uncertainty model, and practical constraints. This perspective has motivated both exact and heuristic solvers, including sequential sensor elimination, convex relaxations, genetic algorithms, and Bayesian experimental design approaches, especially for large-scale civil infrastructure where exhaustive search is infeasible ref [28], ref [31], ref [34], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement
subsections.content:
Optimal sensor placement in SHM is constrained by far more than estimation accuracy. Practical deployments must respect installation and lifecycle cost, power and communication budgets, access limitations, environmental survivability, and maintenance burden. These considerations are especially acute in wireless SHM, where network lifetime, synchronization, packet loss, and onboard computation couple sensing decisions to communication topology and energy management rather than to structural observability alone ref [36], ref [37]. For civil infrastructure, additional constraints arise from traffic control, heritage preservation, corrosion exposure, and the need to retrofit existing assets without interrupting service.

Modeling assumptions also introduce design constraints. Placements optimized for a nominal finite-element model may degrade under modeling error, environmental variability, and operational uncertainty; robust formulations therefore account for uncertainty in modal parameters, excitation, and damage scenarios rather than maximizing a deterministic criterion only ref [38], ref [39]. In large-scale systems, redundancy and fault tolerance become essential because sensor malfunction, drift, and calibration loss can compromise diagnostics over long monitoring horizons ref [40]. These issues motivate formulations that integrate identifiability, reliability, and reconfigurability, sometimes using information-theoretic or Bayesian criteria to balance uncertainty reduction against resource limits ref [41], ref [42].

Implementation further depends on measurement modality and data quality. Accelerometers, strain gauges, fiber-optic sensors, and vision-based systems differ in spatial coverage, bandwidth, noise characteristics, and installation logistics, so feasible locations are often discrete and modality-specific ref [43], ref [44]. Consequently, practical sensor placement is best viewed as a multi-objective design problem in which diagnostic performance must be traded against cost, durability, accessibility, and operability across the monitoring lifecycle ref [45].

subsections.section_title: Optimization Problem Formulations in SHM and Sensor Network Design
subsections.content:
Objective functions in sensor placement for structural health monitoring (SHM) encode what it means for a sensor network to be informative, reliable, and economical. A dominant class maximizes modal identifiability or linear independence of measured responses, often through the Fisher information matrix, its determinant (D-optimality), trace-based criteria, or modal assurance measures. Early formulations based on effective independence (EFI) explicitly retain sensor sets that maximize independence of target mode shapes, while variants use kinetic energy or information entropy to improve robustness to modeling bias and mode truncation ref [46], ref [28], ref [47], ref [48].

A second class defines objectives directly in terms of damage detectability or estimation accuracy. Here, placement is chosen to maximize sensitivity of measurements to stiffness-loss parameters, minimize posterior uncertainty in Bayesian model updating, or optimize classification performance for damage diagnosis ref [49], ref [50]. These formulations are especially relevant when the monitoring objective is not modal testing per se but rapid localization, quantification, or prognosis under sparse instrumentation.

Practical SHM formulations increasingly combine information gain with deployment costs and operational constraints. Typical objectives therefore trade off estimation quality against the number of sensors, wiring or communication burden, energy consumption, and redundancy, often using mutual information or entropy reduction for stochastic fields and wireless sensor networks ref [51], ref [52], ref [53]. Consequently, the objective function largely determines whether the problem is combinatorial, submodular, or multi-objective, and thus which optimization and evaluation methods are appropriate.

subsections.section_title: Optimization Problem Formulations in SHM and Sensor Network Design
subsections.content:
Single-objective formulations remain common in SHM sensor placement when one performance criterion dominates the design brief. Typical objectives maximize information gain or identifiability, often through Fisher information, determinant- or trace-based criteria, modal assurance surrogates, or expected damage-detection capability. Early optimal placement studies for modal testing and identification framed the problem as maximizing linear independence of measured mode shapes or minimizing estimation uncertainty, thereby producing compact discrete optimization models amenable to greedy or combinatorial search methods [1,2]. In SHM-oriented formulations, the same logic is frequently specialized to damage localization accuracy, Bayesian utility, or entropy reduction, yielding a single scalar merit function for ranking candidate layouts [3,4].

Multi-objective formulations arise when informative sensing must be balanced against deployment cost, wiring length, power consumption, robustness to modeling error, or redundancy. Rather than collapsing these factors into a weighted sum, many studies explicitly seek Pareto-optimal sensor sets, revealing trade-offs that are otherwise obscured by scalarization [5,6]. Evolutionary multi-objective algorithms have been especially influential because they can accommodate nonlinear, nonconvex, and mixed discrete-continuous placement models while preserving multiple competing designs for later engineering judgment [7,8]. In wireless SHM, this perspective is particularly important because communication and energy objectives can conflict directly with estimation accuracy [9].

From a formulation standpoint, the choice between single- and multi-objective models affects both interpretability and algorithm selection. Single-objective problems are easier to benchmark and often support stronger theoretical analysis, but they can embed subjective preference information implicitly through normalization or weighting. Multi-objective models better reflect practical SHM decisions under budget and operational constraints, especially in sequential or adaptive monitoring settings, yet require additional decision rules such as Pareto ranking, knee-point selection, or posterior utility assessment to identify implementable solutions [4,6,10].

subsections.section_title: Optimization Problem Formulations in SHM and Sensor Network Design
subsections.subsection_title: Discrete, Continuous, and Mixed Decision Spaces
subsections.content:
A central modeling choice in optimal sensor placement for SHM is the structure of the decision space. In many classical formulations, variables are binary, indicating whether a sensor is installed at a candidate degree of freedom or structural location. This discrete view matches practical procurement and installation decisions and underlies formulations based on modal independence, Fisher information, or information entropy, as seen in effective independence and related methods for large structural systems ref [54], ref [55], ref [56]. Discrete spaces are also natural when accessibility, wiring, and budget constraints restrict placement to a predefined finite set of feasible sites.

Continuous decision spaces arise when sensor coordinates, orientations, interrogation times, or other design variables are not confined to a catalog of candidate locations. Such formulations are less common in civil SHM than binary placement models, but they appear in broader optimal experimental design and Bayesian inference settings where the design variable is spatially continuous and uncertainty reduction is measured through posterior covariance or expected utility ref [57], ref [58]. Continuous models can better represent geometric flexibility, but they typically require nonconvex optimization and repeated solution of forward or inverse problems.

Many realistic SHM designs are therefore mixed: binary variables select the number and type of sensors, while continuous variables tune positions, thresholds, or sampling policies. Mixed spaces are especially important in wireless sensor networks, where placement interacts with communication range, energy consumption, and routing, producing coupled integer-continuous programs ref [59], ref [60]. Similar mixed formulations also appear in multi-type sensor deployment and damage-identification-oriented design, where heterogeneous sensing modalities and parametric constraints must be optimized simultaneously ref [38], ref [61]. The chosen decision-space representation strongly influences algorithm selection, from greedy and submodular methods for discrete placement to evolutionary or surrogate-assisted methods for mixed and continuous designs ref [53].

subsections.section_title: Optimization Problem Formulations in SHM and Sensor Network Design
subsections.content:
Deterministic formulations in structural health monitoring (SHM) and optimal sensor placement assume that structural properties, loading scenarios, and measurement quality are known or represented by nominal values. Under this assumption, optimization commonly targets information-rich layouts through criteria derived from modal independence, observability, or estimation accuracy, such as effective independence or Fisher-information-based measures ref [62], ref [28]. Deterministic models are attractive because they yield compact problem statements and permit efficient combinatorial or mathematical-programming solvers, but their solutions can be sensitive to modeling error, environmental variability, and damage-state uncertainty.

Stochastic formulations explicitly represent uncertainty in structural parameters, excitation, noise, and damage occurrence by optimizing expected utility, probability of correct diagnosis, or robustness over ensembles of scenarios. Bayesian and information-theoretic sensor placement strategies exemplify this shift, where designs are selected to maximize expected information gain or reduce posterior uncertainty in model updating and damage identification ref [63], ref [64]. Related robust placement models also hedge against uncertainty in mode shapes or candidate damage patterns by seeking layouts whose performance degrades minimally under perturbations ref [65], ref [66]. Such formulations are especially relevant when sensing decisions must remain effective across changing operational and environmental conditions.

In practice, the boundary between deterministic and stochastic models is often blurred. Scenario-based optimization, min-max robustness, and reliability-constrained formulations occupy an intermediate space, balancing computational tractability with uncertainty awareness ref [67], ref [68]. For wireless sensor networks used in SHM, stochasticity is further induced by packet loss, energy depletion, and communication failures, motivating probabilistic formulations that couple sensing quality with network reliability and lifetime ref [36]. The resulting modeling choice strongly shapes algorithm selection: deterministic objectives often support greedy ranking or gradient-based search, whereas stochastic formulations typically require sampling, surrogate modeling, or simulation-based optimization.

subsections.section_title: Optimization Problem Formulations in SHM and Sensor Network Design
subsections.content:
Static placement strategies determine all sensor locations before deployment and are typically justified when structural properties, excitation scenarios, and budget constraints are assumed fixed over the monitoring horizon. In SHM, such formulations often maximize modal independence, Fisher information, or damage-detectability surrogates under a one-shot design paradigm, as exemplified by effective independence and related pre-test methods for modal testing and damage identification ref [28], ref [69], ref [70]. Their main advantage is computational simplicity and ease of implementation, but the resulting designs can be sensitive to modeling error, environmental variability, and sensor failures.

Adaptive placement strategies instead treat sensing as a sequential decision process in which measurements collected at earlier stages update the structural model, uncertainty description, or posterior damage probabilities, and subsequent sensor actions are chosen accordingly. This idea is closely connected to Bayesian experimental design and information-driven monitoring, where sensor relocation or activation is selected to maximize expected entropy reduction, mutual information, or posterior utility ref [71], ref [72], ref [42]. In wireless sensor networks for SHM, adaptation also appears as dynamic scheduling or topology reconfiguration to balance information quality with energy and communication limits ref [36], ref [73].

The static-versus-adaptive distinction therefore changes the optimization model itself: static schemes solve a single-stage combinatorial program, whereas adaptive schemes are naturally formulated as multistage stochastic, Bayesian, or partially observed control problems. Adaptive methods can achieve greater robustness to epistemic uncertainty and evolving damage states, but they incur substantially higher online computational and logistical costs. Consequently, many practical frameworks adopt hybrid strategies: an initially optimized static baseline is deployed, then refined through periodic updating, sparse mobile sensing, or event-triggered rescheduling ref [42], ref [73], ref [74].

subsections.section_title: Taxonomy of Optimization Algorithms for SHM Applications
subsections.content:
Classical mathematical programming methods form the earliest rigorous layer of optimization in structural health monitoring (SHM), especially for sensor placement, model updating, and damage parameter estimation. Their defining feature is the explicit use of objective functions and constraints derived from mechanics, observability, or information measures, enabling deterministic search and, in some cases, optimality guarantees. In optimal sensor placement, these methods commonly maximize Fisher information, modal independence, or observability metrics under cardinality, geometric, and cost constraints. A seminal line of work used effective independence and related matrix-rank criteria to prune candidate locations while preserving modal identifiability ref [75], and closely related formulations based on kinetic energy or information entropy were later developed for practical placement design ref [76], ref [77].

For SHM inverse problems, classical formulations typically appear as constrained least-squares, quadratic programming, linear/nonlinear programming, or semidefinite relaxations. Such models are attractive when damage variables are continuous and the forward model is differentiable, because convexity or local smoothness can be exploited for efficient solution. Early studies on optimal instrumentation of large civil structures demonstrated how integer or mixed discrete-continuous programming can encode budget and redundancy constraints directly ref [78], while information-theoretic design criteria for dynamic system identification provided a principled basis for D-, A-, and E-optimal placement rules ref [79].

Despite their analytical clarity, purely classical methods face well-known limitations in SHM: nonconvexity induced by combinatorial placement decisions, sensitivity to modeling error, and scalability issues for high-dimensional finite-element models. These concerns motivated branch-and-bound and relaxation strategies for discrete sensor selection ref [80], as well as sparse reconstruction viewpoints that recast damage localization or sensing design into regularized optimization problems ref [81], ref [82]. Consequently, classical programming remains foundational not because it solves every SHM optimization problem outright, but because it provides the benchmark formulations, constraint handling mechanisms, and optimality concepts on which later heuristic, hybrid, and learning-assisted methods are built ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Taxonomy of Optimization Algorithms for SHM Applications
subsections.content:
Gradient-based and sensitivity-driven approaches occupy an important niche in structural health monitoring (SHM) optimization when the objective and constraints can be expressed through differentiable response models. In damage identification, these methods typically minimize residuals between measured and predicted modal, static, or frequency-response quantities, while in sensor placement they optimize information-theoretic or estimation metrics under placement constraints. Their efficiency derives from local derivative information, obtained analytically, by direct differentiation of finite-element equations, or through adjoint formulations that decouple gradient cost from the number of design variables ref [1], ref [83], ref [84].

A central stream of work computes structural response sensitivities with respect to stiffness, mass, or elemental damage parameters and embeds them in iterative updating algorithms. Modal sensitivity formulations for damage localization and quantification were established early and remain influential because they link physical parameter changes to measurable eigenproperties ref [85], ref [86]. For larger inverse problems, finite-element model updating based on sensitivity matrices and regularized least-squares formulations has been used to improve numerical stability and identifiability in noisy settings ref [87], ref [88]. In sensor placement, gradient information has likewise been exploited to maximize Fisher information or related criteria, especially when continuous relaxations are adopted before discretization ref [89].

Despite their favorable convergence speed near smooth optima, these methods are intrinsically local and can degrade under multimodal objectives, severe nonlinearity, modeling error, or binary placement decisions. Consequently, SHM studies often combine sensitivity analysis with regularization, trust-region or sequential quadratic programming strategies, and occasionally with global search layers. More recent work extends differentiable optimization to topology-oriented sensor layout and PDE-constrained inverse damage problems, indicating that gradient-based schemes remain highly competitive whenever reliable derivatives and adequate initialization are available ref [83], ref [84], ref [90].

subsections.section_title: Taxonomy of Optimization Algorithms for SHM Applications
subsections.content:
Heuristic and metaheuristic algorithms are widely used in structural health monitoring (SHM), especially for optimal sensor placement and damage-identification problems that are combinatorial, nonconvex, noisy, or multimodal. In contrast to gradient-based methods, they search through probabilistic variation, adaptive memory, or population interaction, making them attractive when the objective involves modal independence, information entropy, or model-updating residuals with discrete design constraints. Simulated annealing and tabu search provided early general frameworks for escaping local minima in difficult combinatorial spaces, while genetic algorithms established a flexible encoding-and-selection paradigm that has been repeatedly adapted to sensor-network design in structural systems [1, ref 2, ref 3].

Within SHM-oriented optimization, genetic and evolutionary schemes are particularly common because candidate sensor layouts can be naturally represented as binary strings and evaluated using criteria such as the effective independence method, Fisher information matrix measures, or modal assurance indicators. Particle swarm optimization offers a lower-parameter population search with rapid empirical convergence, whereas ant colony optimization is well suited to discrete placement and routing-style formulations [4, ref 5]. Comparative studies in civil infrastructure monitoring have shown that these methods can outperform greedy elimination strategies when higher-order interactions among candidate locations are important, although solution quality remains sensitive to representation, penalty handling, and stopping rules [6, ref 7].

The main trade-off is that metaheuristics improve robustness to nonconvexity at the expense of weaker theoretical guarantees and higher computational cost, especially when each fitness evaluation requires finite-element analysis or uncertainty propagation. Consequently, SHM applications increasingly combine them with surrogate models, local refinements, or physics-based initialization. Their practical value lies less in universal optimality than in delivering high-quality feasible designs for large, constrained structural systems where exact search is prohibitive [3, ref 5, ref 8].

subsections.section_title: Taxonomy of Optimization Algorithms for SHM Applications
subsections.content:
Hybrid and memetic optimization frameworks combine complementary search mechanisms to address the mixed discrete–continuous, highly nonconvex character of structural health monitoring (SHM) inverse problems and optimal sensor placement. In this context, a global metaheuristic is typically used to explore broad design spaces, while a local improvement stage refines promising candidates using gradient, surrogate, or problem-specific neighborhood moves. The memetic paradigm of coupling population-based evolution with individual learning was formalized by Moscato and Cotta and later systematized in reviews of memetic computing, which provide the conceptual basis for many SHM-oriented hybrids ref [99], ref [100]. Such designs are especially attractive when objective functions are multimodal, noisy, or expensive because they can improve exploitation without sacrificing the robustness of global exploration.

Within sensor placement and model updating, hybridization often appears as GA-based search combined with local repair, sequential elimination, or sensitivity-guided refinement. For example, Papadimitriou developed information-theoretic formulations for optimal sensor placement in structural dynamics that naturally support sequential and hybrid search strategies under observability and uncertainty constraints ref [101]. Yi et al. used a multi-objective genetic algorithm for optimal sensor placement on high-rise buildings, illustrating how evolutionary search can be paired with engineering constraints and post-processing to obtain practical layouts ref [102]. In damage identification, hybrid neural-network/genetic approaches were explored early by Chou and Ghaboussi, while Levin and Lieven combined genetic search with neural-network approximations to accelerate structural optimization, anticipating later surrogate-assisted SHM hybrids ref [103], ref [104].

More recent hybrid frameworks in structural optimization and inverse analysis integrate evolutionary or swarm search with approximation models, decomposition, or local search to reduce computational cost and improve convergence reliability. Simpson et al. reviewed approximation methods in multidisciplinary design optimization, a foundation for surrogate-assisted hybrids widely transferable to SHM updating and placement tasks ref [105]. Jin surveyed fitness approximation in evolutionary computation, clarifying when surrogate-enhanced memetic schemes are most effective for expensive simulations ref [106]. In parallel, Talbi provided a taxonomy of hybrid metaheuristics, and Gandomi et al. reviewed benchmarked hybrid evolutionary approaches in engineering optimization, both of which are directly relevant for selecting exploration–exploitation balances in large-scale SHM applications ref [107], ref [10]. Overall, hybrid and memetic methods are best viewed as architecture-level strategies that tailor optimization operators to structural physics, uncertainty, and computational budget.

subsections.section_title: Taxonomy of Optimization Algorithms for SHM Applications
subsections.content:
Machine learning-assisted optimization in structural health monitoring (SHM) augments, rather than replaces, classical and metaheuristic search. The main role of learning is to reduce the cost of repeated structural analyses, guide exploration of high-dimensional design spaces, or infer informative sensor configurations from data. A common pattern is surrogate-assisted optimization, where expensive finite-element or reliability evaluations are emulated by response surfaces such as kriging or other Gaussian-process models, enabling efficient sequential design and uncertainty-aware search ref [108], ref [109]. Related Bayesian optimization ideas are especially attractive when objective evaluations are scarce and noisy, because acquisition functions explicitly balance exploitation and exploration ref [110].

In SHM and optimal sensor placement, learned surrogates have been coupled with vibration-based model updating and reliability analysis to accelerate inverse identification and damage-sensitive design loops. Early SHM-oriented studies showed that neural networks can emulate structural response mappings for model updating ref [111], while kriging-based reliability methods demonstrated how active learning can focus evaluations near limit states or informative regions of the design space ref [112], ref [113]. For sensor placement more specifically, machine learning also serves as a feature-selection engine: sparse regression and regularization-based learning can identify compact measurement sets while preserving reconstructability or classification accuracy, linking placement to compressed sensing and dictionary learning ideas ref [114], ref [115].

Recent work further integrates deep learning with optimization by using graph neural networks or reinforcement learning to exploit structural topology and sequential decision making. Graph-based models have been proposed for sensor placement on irregular structural graphs, learning transferable policies over candidate layouts ref [116], whereas deep reinforcement learning has been used to construct placement strategies through reward-driven interaction with structural simulators ref [117]. Despite these advances, their practical value depends on training-data quality, generalization across structural classes, and the preservation of engineering constraints; consequently, machine learning-assisted optimization is most effective when embedded in hybrid frameworks with physics-based validation and uncertainty quantification.

subsections.section_title: Taxonomy of Optimization Algorithms for SHM Applications
subsections.content:
Comparative evaluation of optimization algorithms for structural health monitoring (SHM) and optimal sensor placement is most informative when framed in terms of search-space structure, computational burden, and robustness to modeling uncertainty. Classical gradient-based formulations are attractive when objective and constraint functions are smooth and sensitivities can be computed efficiently; this is evident in information-based sensor placement formulations derived from Fisher information or Bayesian criteria, which often admit principled local updates but may suffer from nonconvexity and dependence on initial guesses ref [118], ref [119]. By contrast, combinatorial formulations based on effective independence or modal criteria emphasize algebraic transparency and low implementation complexity, but their greedy or sequential nature can become suboptimal under multiple competing objectives ref [120], ref [121].

Heuristic and metaheuristic methods broaden the search beyond local basins and are therefore useful for discrete, nonlinear, and constrained SHM design spaces. Genetic algorithms, ant colony optimization, and particle swarm optimization have all been reported to handle multimodal sensor placement landscapes and damage-identification inverse problems with limited derivative information ref [122], ref [123], ref [124]. Their main trade-off is higher function-evaluation cost and weaker guarantees of global optimality, especially when each candidate requires repeated finite-element analyses. Practical comparisons therefore favor algorithms that balance diversification with problem-specific exploitation, or that incorporate reduced-order models and surrogate evaluations to improve scalability ref [123], ref [125].

A recurring conclusion in the literature is that no single optimizer dominates across all SHM tasks. Performance depends on variable type (continuous versus discrete), objective topology, noise level, and budget for repeated simulations. Comparative studies in sensor placement and damage detection increasingly advocate hybrid workflows that combine mathematically grounded initialization, sensitivity information, and population-based global search, while benchmarking with application-relevant criteria such as identifiability, sparsity, and computational time rather than best objective value alone ref [119], ref [125], ref [126].

subsections.section_title: Performance Criteria, Evaluation Metrics, and Benchmarking Protocols
subsections.content:
In SHM-oriented sensor placement and algorithm evaluation, observability concerns whether the measured responses contain sufficient information to reconstruct structural states or modal coordinates, whereas identifiability asks whether damage-sensitive parameters can be uniquely inferred from those measurements. Early optimal placement studies therefore used modal independence and estimation quality as proxies for information content, notably via the effective independence method and related Fisher-information formulations that maximize linear independence of target mode shapes or minimize parameter covariance under candidate layouts [1], ref [128], ref [56]. These criteria remain influential because they connect placement decisions directly to estimation-theoretic limits rather than only to geometric coverage.

Information content is now commonly quantified through the Fisher information matrix, its determinant or trace, entropy-based measures, and Bayesian utility functions. D-optimality and related criteria reward layouts that reduce posterior uncertainty in model updating and damage identification, while mutual-information formulations explicitly value sensors that maximize expected reduction in uncertainty about latent structural states or parameters [4], ref [130], ref [131]. For vibration-based SHM, these metrics are often evaluated on modal features, strain responses, or sparse state-space models, and can reveal trade-offs between global observability and local identifiability when damage scenarios are spatially correlated or only weakly excite selected modes.

A recurring benchmarking issue is that high observability of undamaged dynamics does not guarantee high damage identifiability. Accordingly, more recent evaluation protocols compare layouts using inverse-problem performance indicators such as posterior variance, parameter correlation, condition number, or probability of correct damage scenario discrimination under model uncertainty [7], ref [132], ref [133]. For fair comparison, surveys should distinguish criteria aimed at preserving modal basis quality from those tailored to damage-feature separability, since the latter better reflect decision-relevant information content in practical SHM deployments [10].

subsections.section_title: Performance Criteria, Evaluation Metrics, and Benchmarking Protocols
subsections.content:
Damage-detection and localization performance is typically assessed by treating sensor layouts and inference algorithms as classifiers or estimators over damage presence, extent, and position. Common detection metrics include probability of detection, false-alarm rate, receiver-operating-characteristic behavior, and confusion-matrix summaries such as precision, recall, and F1 score when multiple damage classes are considered. In vibration-based SHM, these metrics are often tied to changes in modal features or flexibility indicators, while in novelty-detection settings they are evaluated under baseline-versus-damaged discrimination tasks ref [13], ref [135], ref [136].

Localization performance requires stronger criteria than detection alone. Studies commonly report spatial error between estimated and true damage locations, region-of-interest hit rate, ranking accuracy of candidate elements, and success within a tolerance radius or finite-element substructure. For guided-wave and impedance-based methods, localization is frequently benchmarked by imaging quality, centroid error, and damage index contrast, whereas model-based inverse methods may quantify estimation bias and variance in identified stiffness-loss parameters ref [16], ref [137], ref [138]. In sensor placement studies, these measures should be normalized by structure size and candidate sensor count so that gains in localization can be compared fairly across layouts.

A recurring lesson from benchmark investigations is that high detectability does not guarantee reliable localization, especially for small damage, symmetric structures, or sparse networks. Accordingly, evaluation protocols should separate binary detection from localization accuracy, report performance under multiple damage severities and positions, and include uncertainty bands over repeated noise realizations or environmental variations ref [139], ref [1], ref [140]. This is particularly important because environmental and operational variability can mask damage-sensitive features and inflate apparent localization performance if testing is restricted to idealized conditions ref [141].

subsections.section_title: Performance Criteria, Evaluation Metrics, and Benchmarking Protocols
subsections.subsection_title: Cost, Energy, and Network Efficiency Metrics
subsections.content:
Beyond detection accuracy, SHM sensor-placement and network-design studies increasingly evaluate economic and operational efficiency. Cost metrics are typically formulated as total installed cost or life-cycle cost, combining sensor procurement, cabling, installation, data acquisition, maintenance, and in some cases inspection savings; this viewpoint is especially important in wireless and large-scale civil infrastructure, where communication and deployment overhead can dominate hardware cost [1], ref [142]. In optimization formulations, cost is therefore often treated as an explicit objective or budget constraint alongside information-based criteria, yielding Pareto trade-offs between monitoring quality and resource expenditure [3], ref [45].

Energy-aware metrics are central for wireless SHM because node lifetime depends on sensing, local processing, radio transmission, and duty-cycling strategy. Accordingly, common measures include per-node and network-wide power consumption, expected battery lifetime, communication load, latency, and the number of transmissions needed for event detection or modal estimation [1], ref [144]. Closely related network-efficiency indicators include coverage/connectivity, robustness to packet loss, synchronization burden, and scalability with respect to node count, all of which affect the practical utility of dense smart-sensor deployments [6], ref [37].

Recent benchmarking practice therefore favors multi-objective assessment rather than single-score reporting: algorithms are compared by information gain per sensor, detection or identification performance under fixed budget, and lifetime-aware utility under realistic communication architectures [3], ref [144], ref [146]. For fair comparison, studies should state whether cost models include wiring versus wireless infrastructure, centralized versus decentralized computation, and whether energy estimates are based on radio models, measured hardware consumption, or simplified proxy counts, since these assumptions materially change the ranking of competing placement strategies [2], ref [37], ref [73].

subsections.section_title: Performance Criteria, Evaluation Metrics, and Benchmarking Protocols
subsections.content:
Robustness under noise and uncertainty is a central evaluation criterion because SHM decisions are often made from sparse, noisy, and environmentally variable measurements. Accordingly, benchmarking should report performance degradation as signal-to-noise ratio decreases, as modeling errors increase, and as operational/environmental variability induces feature drift. Early vibration-based studies showed that damage-sensitive features can be strongly confounded by temperature and other changing conditions, implying that an algorithm that performs well in nominal simulations may fail in deployment unless uncertainty is explicitly represented in the evaluation protocol ref [1], ref [147].

In practice, robustness is commonly quantified through probability of detection, false-alarm rate, receiver-operating characteristics, and uncertainty bounds on identified parameters or damage indices under repeated noisy trials. Statistical pattern-recognition frameworks have emphasized novelty-detection thresholds and outlier analysis under uncertain baselines ref [148], while Bayesian model updating and inference provide posterior credible intervals and natural mechanisms for propagating measurement and modeling uncertainty to damage decisions ref [133], ref [149]. For sensor placement, robustness assessment should therefore test whether candidate layouts preserve detectability and localization accuracy when sensor readings are corrupted, missing, or biased, rather than only under deterministic forward models ref [32], ref [150].

A rigorous protocol should also distinguish aleatory measurement noise from epistemic uncertainty in structural parameters, boundary conditions, and environmental loading. Robust algorithms are increasingly validated through Monte Carlo simulation, stochastic finite-element models, and environmental/operational variability compensation methods such as cointegration or low-dimensional latent representations ref [147], ref [151], ref [152]. More recent probabilistic SHM reviews further recommend reporting calibration quality, uncertainty decomposition, and cross-condition generalization so that claimed gains are not limited to a single noise realization or laboratory condition ref [153].

subsections.section_title: Performance Criteria, Evaluation Metrics, and Benchmarking Protocols
subsections.content:
Benchmarking in structural health monitoring (SHM) optimization is strongest when algorithms are tested on common structures, loading cases, and sensing models rather than on isolated, study-specific simulations. Widely used physical benchmarks include the IASC-ASCE phase I and phase II steel-frame testbeds, which were explicitly developed to compare damage detection methods under controlled stiffness-loss scenarios and measurement noise ref [154], ref [155]. For bridge SHM, full-scale monitored structures such as the Alamosa Canyon Bridge and the Z24 Bridge have become important reference cases because they expose algorithms to environmental variability, operational uncertainty, and realistic sensor layouts ref [156], ref [157].

Simulation platforms complement scarce experimental benchmarks by enabling repeatable studies of sensor placement, observability, and inverse identification. In practice, finite-element models of canonical beams, trusses, and multi-story frames remain dominant, often reduced through modal truncation or substructuring to make optimization tractable. Community software has also improved comparability: OpenSees provides a widely adopted open framework for nonlinear structural simulation and damage scenario generation ref [158], while benchmark-oriented studies in wireless sensing frequently use instrumented laboratory structures such as the LANL three-story frame to evaluate networked SHM strategies under realistic communication and power constraints ref [159].

A persistent limitation is that many "benchmarks" differ in damage parameterization, excitation assumptions, and noise injection, making cross-paper comparison difficult. More rigorous protocols therefore favor public datasets, explicit train/test splits across environmental conditions, and validation on both numerical and experimental platforms. This trend is reflected in benchmark data resources from long-term bridge monitoring and vibration-based damage identification studies, including Z24 and the Tianjin Yonghe Bridge, as well as comparative reviews emphasizing standardized testbeds for objective assessment ref [157], ref [160], ref [1], ref [161].

Overall, effective benchmarking should span three levels: idealized numerical models for algorithmic screening, laboratory structures for controlled repeatability, and full-scale fielded systems for ecological validity. Reporting the structural model, boundary conditions, excitation type, sensor topology, and data availability is essential if optimization and sensor placement methods are to be reproducible and meaningfully compared across the SHM literature ref [158], ref [161], ref [162].

subsections.section_title: Performance Criteria, Evaluation Metrics, and Benchmarking Protocols
subsections.content:
Reproducibility in SHM optimization and sensor placement studies depends on more than reporting a final sensor layout or objective value. Authors should specify the structural model, candidate sensor set, excitation and noise assumptions, optimization budget, stopping criteria, and random seeds, since stochastic search can produce materially different solutions across runs. The broader reproducibility concerns identified in computational science and optimization are directly relevant here: insufficient disclosure of algorithms and implementation details impedes independent verification and fair comparison ref [163], ref [164], ref [165]. In SHM, open benchmark data and code repositories have therefore become increasingly important complements to journal articles ref [166], ref [167].

Statistical validation is equally necessary because many placement and model-updating methods are evaluated on limited case studies and under a single realization of noise or damage. Performance should be summarized over repeated trials, cross-validation splits, or Monte Carlo simulations, with effect sizes and uncertainty intervals rather than isolated best-case results. Established statistical tools for classifier comparison and repeated-experiment analysis, such as cross-validation based tests and multiple-comparison procedures, are useful when comparing damage detection pipelines or optimization heuristics ref [168], ref [169]. Recent methodological work in machine learning further cautions against over-interpreting average ranks or point estimates without paired statistical analysis and variance reporting ref [170], ref [171].

For this literature, a minimum reporting standard should include the number of independent runs, dispersion measures for each metric, treatment of hyperparameter tuning, and explicit separation between training, validation, and test scenarios. When experimental data are scarce, bootstrap or resampling-based uncertainty quantification can still provide defensible confidence statements ref [172]. Such practices would make claims of superiority more credible and would substantially improve the comparability of SHM sensor placement studies.

subsections.section_title: Application Domains and Case Study Patterns
subsections.content:
Civil infrastructure has been the dominant application domain for optimization-based structural health monitoring (SHM) and sensor placement because bridges, buildings, towers, and lifeline systems combine large spatial extent, limited instrumentation budgets, and strong environmental variability. In this setting, optimization is typically used to balance information gain against installation and maintenance constraints, often through modal observability, Fisher-information, entropy, or effective-independence criteria. Early bridge-focused studies established that optimal layouts can substantially improve modal identification and damage sensitivity compared with heuristic deployment, particularly when only a small number of channels is feasible ref [28], ref [173], ref [89].

A recurring pattern in civil case studies is the coupling of placement objectives with uncertain operational conditions. Ambient-vibration identification under traffic, wind, and temperature variations motivates robust formulations that seek sensor sets informative across multiple model realizations rather than for a single nominal finite-element model ref [38], ref [96]. This is especially important for long-span bridges and large buildings, where model reduction, accessibility of mounting locations, cable routing, and power supply constraints materially alter the admissible search space ref [7], ref [174]. Consequently, practical deployments often use optimization only after aggressive pre-screening of feasible nodes and sensing modalities.

Another consistent lesson is that methods transfer across civil subclasses more readily at the level of objective design than at the level of exact algorithms. Effective-independence and information-theoretic criteria developed for modal testing remain influential, but field deployments increasingly integrate wireless sensing, decentralized acquisition, and lifecycle considerations such as communication cost and battery usage ref [1], ref [36]. Landmark full-scale implementations on structures such as the Tsing Ma Bridge and the Golden Gate Bridge illustrate this transition from purely identification-oriented placement toward network-aware SHM architectures intended for continuous operation ref [174], ref [175].

subsections.section_title: Application Domains and Case Study Patterns
subsections.content:
In aerospace and precision mechanical structures, sensor placement is typically driven by stringent mass, wiring, and power constraints, so optimization is closely tied to modal observability and parameter-identification objectives rather than simple coverage. Early work established effective-independence and related Fisher-information criteria for selecting accelerometer locations that preserve target mode shapes in flexible airframes and space structures ref [176], ref [28]. These ideas were generalized to robust formulations that account for model uncertainty and test-analysis correlation, which is crucial because aerospace structures often exhibit closely spaced modes, lightweight damping, and configuration-dependent boundary conditions ref [177], ref [178].

A recurring case-study pattern is the use of reduced-order finite-element models combined with combinatorial or heuristic search to place a small number of sensors on wings, trusses, panels, or rotating machinery components. For damage detection, optimization often targets sensitivity of measured responses to stiffness loss or delamination, using modal strain energy, residual flexibility, or Bayesian utility as placement criteria ref [162], ref [179]. In mechanical systems with active vibration control, placement of collocated or near-collocated sensor-actuator pairs further couples monitoring and control objectives, leading to criteria based on controllability-observability balancing rather than diagnosis alone ref [180].

Compared with civil structures, transferability is mixed: the mathematical criteria are portable, but aerospace applications are more sensitive to high modal density, operational variability, and certification-driven requirements for redundancy and fault tolerance. Wireless approaches remain less dominant than in civil SHM because of electromagnetic, reliability, and maintenance constraints, although distributed sensing concepts such as guided-wave and dense piezoelectric networks have been explored for aircraft skin and composite panels ref [181], ref [139]. Consequently, aerospace and mechanical studies often serve as a proving ground for high-fidelity model-based optimization, while field-scale adoption depends on demonstrating robustness under realistic operational environments ref [182].

subsections.section_title: Application Domains and Case Study Patterns
subsections.content:
Energy and offshore systems pose a distinctive sensor-placement problem because monitoring objectives are coupled to harsh environments, sparse accessibility, and strongly operationally driven loads. In offshore wind turbines and support structures, optimization is commonly framed around joint estimation of modal properties, fatigue-relevant responses, and damage-sensitive features under significant environmental and operational variability. Case studies on offshore wind support structures therefore often combine reduced-order structural models with information-based criteria or model-updating objectives rather than relying only on classical mode-shape coverage metrics [1], [2].

For fixed and floating offshore platforms, sensor layouts must also respect marine installation constraints, cable routing, power availability, and survivability under corrosion and hydrodynamic loading. This has encouraged robust placement formulations that trade nominal identifiability against redundancy and fault tolerance, especially when monitoring is intended for long-term integrity management rather than short-term testing [3], [4]. A related pattern in oil, gas, and subsea systems is the integration of SHM with digital-twin or Bayesian updating workflows, where sensor locations are selected to reduce uncertainty in fatigue hot spots, joint dynamics, or mooring-line states instead of maximizing a purely geometric observability index [5], [6].

Across energy assets more broadly, recurring lessons are that transferable optimization ideas exist, but objective functions are domain-specific: wind-turbine blades emphasize strain and aeroelastic state reconstruction, offshore jackets emphasize global-local fatigue interaction, and pipelines or risers emphasize distributed sensing for leak, vibration, or free-span detection [7], [8], [9]. Consequently, methods imported from civil infrastructure are most successful when augmented with environmental robustness, maintenance logistics, and lifecycle cost considerations [10].

subsections.section_title: Application Domains and Case Study Patterns
subsections.content:
Wireless and distributed sensor networks shift sensor-placement optimization from a purely information-theoretic problem to a joint design problem involving communication reliability, synchronization, bandwidth, and node energy. Early SHM deployments demonstrated that low-power wireless sensing can support modal identification and event-based monitoring at meaningful scales, but also revealed practical penalties from packet loss, clock drift, and limited onboard computation [1], [2]. Consequently, placement objectives in wireless SHM often augment observability or Fisher-information criteria with constraints on network connectivity, hop count, and expected lifetime, rather than treating measurement quality in isolation.

A recurring pattern is the move toward decentralized or hierarchical architectures in which local processing reduces communication load. Middleware and embedded platforms such as Narada and subsequent cyber-physical implementations enabled in-network interrogation, damage feature extraction, and adaptive triggering, making dense deployments more feasible on large civil structures [3], [4]. These developments also encouraged optimization formulations that co-design sensing and communication layers, for example by balancing modal coverage against radio topology robustness or by selecting gateway locations jointly with sensor nodes [5], [6]. In this setting, redundancy is valuable not only for estimation accuracy but also for resilience to node or link failures.

Case studies further show that wireless SHM methods transfer unevenly across domains. Civil infrastructure applications benefit from spatial density and ease of retrofit, whereas rotating or metallic systems face harsher electromagnetic and power constraints. Reviews of wireless SHM consistently identify energy harvesting, compressed or decentralized inference, and probabilistic treatment of missing data as key enablers for field deployment [7], [8]. More broadly, the sensor-network literature provides mature optimization tools for coverage-connectivity tradeoffs and lifetime maximization that are increasingly being adapted to SHM-specific objectives [9].

The overarching lesson is that in distributed SHM, an 'optimal' sensor layout is inseparable from the network architecture that sustains it: placements that are near-optimal for model updating or damage localization may be infeasible unless communication and energy constraints are embedded directly into the optimization loop.

subsections.section_title: Application Domains and Case Study Patterns
subsections.content:
A persistent pattern in the SHM optimization literature is the gap between laboratory validation and field deployment. In laboratory studies, optimal sensor placement and related inverse methods are usually tested on well-instrumented benchmark structures with controlled excitation, high signal-to-noise ratio, and stable boundary conditions, such as the IASC-ASCE Phase II benchmark and the Z24 bridge data sets ref [154], ref [200]. Under these conditions, modal identifiability, damage localization, and information-theoretic placement criteria often perform close to their theoretical expectations. Laboratory campaigns have therefore been essential for comparing effective independence, Fisher-information, and modal kinetic energy based formulations before moving to operational systems ref [201], ref [202].

Field deployment introduces nonstationary loading, environmental and operational variability, communication constraints, sensor faults, and limited opportunities for reconfiguration. Long-term bridge and building monitoring programs have shown that temperature, traffic, and aging can dominate modal changes, complicating optimization objectives that are straightforward in the laboratory ref [203], ref [204]. Wireless implementations add further trade-offs between estimation accuracy, synchronization, power consumption, and packet loss, so placement strategies must often co-optimize sensing and networking rather than structural observability alone ref [205], ref [196]. These realities explain why algorithms validated on small laboratory frames may transfer only partially to full-scale infrastructure.

Accordingly, successful field studies tend to use robust, staged workflows: initial model-based placement, pilot deployment, data-driven updating, and periodic reassessment of network utility. Practical demonstrations on large bridges and operational aerospace structures suggest that optimization is most transferable when uncertainty, environmental compensation, and maintainability are built into the objective from the outset rather than treated as post-processing issues ref [203], ref [206], ref [207].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Open Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Digital Twins and Real-Time Adaptive Monitoring
subsections.content:
Digital twins are reshaping structural health monitoring (SHM) from periodic assessment toward continuously updated, decision-oriented representations of assets. In civil infrastructure, the concept couples physics-based models, sensing streams, and state-estimation algorithms so that model parameters, boundary conditions, and damage indicators can be revised online rather than fixed a priori ref [208], ref [209]. This shift is especially relevant to sensor placement and optimization because informative sensing is no longer static: sensing policies can be adapted as the twin identifies regions of high epistemic uncertainty, evolving loads, or emerging anomalies.

A central research direction is real-time adaptive monitoring, where model updating, anomaly detection, and sensing actions are closed in the loop. Recent work on cyber-physical and Bayesian digital twins emphasizes streaming data assimilation, probabilistic calibration, and recursive state estimation for operational decision support ref [210], ref [211]. For vibration-based SHM, sequential Monte Carlo, Kalman filtering, and surrogate-assisted updating have demonstrated how latent structural states can be tracked under nonstationary environments, but scaling these methods to large finite-element models remains challenging ref [212], ref [213]. Consequently, reduced-order modeling, edge/cloud partitioning, and event-triggered sensing are becoming essential for practical deployment.

Open problems concern robustness, trustworthiness, and interoperability. Digital twins must remain reliable under sensor faults, model-form mismatch, and sparse observations, while still supporting timely adaptation of sensor duty cycles, mobile sensing trajectories, or reconfiguration of wireless networks ref [214], ref [74]. Future progress will likely depend on integrating semantic information models with operational SHM pipelines and on linking twin uncertainty directly to control and maintenance actions, as envisioned in broader digital-twin frameworks for the built environment ref [209], ref [215].

references

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Open Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
A central frontier in structural health monitoring (SHM) optimization is the fusion of physics-based models with data-driven inference so that sensor placement, feature extraction, and decision-making remain both accurate and interpretable. Purely data-driven methods can be highly predictive yet brittle under domain shift, sparse damage examples, and changing operational conditions, whereas physics-based strategies may be robust but computationally restrictive or vulnerable to model-form error. Hybrid formulations attempt to overcome this divide by embedding governing mechanics, structural constraints, or latent state-space structure into learning pipelines, as exemplified by physics-informed neural networks and related scientific machine-learning frameworks that enforce differential equations during training [1,2]. For inverse problems relevant to SHM, such integration is especially attractive because it enables damage-sensitive estimation from incomplete and noisy measurements while reducing dependence on exhaustive labeled datasets [3].

Recent work suggests that the most promising fusion strategies are not simply model-assisted classifiers, but closed-loop architectures in which finite-element models, Bayesian updating, sparse sensing, and deep representation learning co-evolve. Data-centric methods such as Gaussian-process latent force models provide one principled mechanism for injecting mechanistic priors into stochastic learning [4], while Bayesian model updating remains a mature route for reconciling measured and simulated response under uncertainty [5]. In parallel, hybrid deep-learning approaches have shown that combining simulated and measured vibration responses can improve damage identification and transferability across loading scenarios [6,7]. These directions are closely aligned with digital twin concepts, where continuously updated physics surrogates and streaming data support online state estimation and prognosis [8].

Open challenges concern scale, trustworthiness, and optimization under uncertainty. Physics-informed losses may be difficult to balance against data fidelity, especially for nonlinear, heterogeneous, or poorly instrumented civil infrastructure; moreover, biased simulators can transfer errors directly into learned models. Future research should therefore emphasize multi-fidelity fusion, active learning for informative sensor reconfiguration, and reliability-aware hybrid inference that explicitly propagates epistemic and aleatory uncertainties [2,5,9]. Progress will likely depend on benchmark problems that pair high-quality experimental data with validated numerical twins, enabling rigorous comparison of fusion strategies for placement and diagnosis tasks [8,10].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Open Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Scalability to Large and Complex Structural Systems
subsections.content:
Scalability remains a central barrier in optimization-driven SHM and sensor placement because objective evaluation becomes prohibitively expensive as structural dimensionality, sensing candidates, and damage scenarios grow. Early information-theoretic and model-based formulations already exposed the combinatorial nature of large-network placement problems and the need for computationally efficient surrogates, sparse parameterizations, or decomposition strategies ref [225], ref [226]. For large civil infrastructure, the challenge is amplified by multi-hazard loading, heterogeneous components, and distributed sensing architectures, which make brute-force finite-element updating or exhaustive placement search impractical.

Promising directions therefore couple structural model reduction with scalable optimization. Proper orthogonal decomposition and Krylov/substructuring ideas can compress high-fidelity dynamics while preserving damage-sensitive features, enabling repeated optimization or Bayesian updating on reduced spaces ref [227], ref [228]. On the placement side, convex relaxation and greedy algorithms with performance guarantees offer tractable alternatives to exhaustive search for large sensor candidate sets, particularly when the objective is tied to observability, estimation error covariance, or submodular information gain ref [229], ref [53]. Wireless sensor network studies further show that scalability must be treated jointly with communication cost, synchronization, and decentralized inference rather than sensing performance alone ref [36].

Future work should move beyond single-structure demonstrations toward graph-based, hierarchical, and federated formulations suited to portfolios of bridges, buildings, and offshore assets. Recent graph neural network approaches for structural response modeling suggest a route to transferable surrogates across topologies and scales ref [230], while digital-twin frameworks for operational infrastructure highlight the need for continual model updating under streaming data and limited computational budgets ref [231]. A key open problem is to integrate such scalable learning architectures with reliability-aware optimization so that approximation error does not undermine decision quality in safety-critical systems.

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Open Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
A persistent limitation in SHM-oriented optimization is the treatment of sensing, model updating, and damage inference as deterministic problems, even though measurement noise, environmental variability, modeling error, and operational uncertainty strongly affect decision quality. Reliability-aware design therefore requires explicit uncertainty quantification (UQ) in both forward prediction and inverse identification, building on probabilistic model classes and Bayesian inference for structural dynamics and damage assessment ref [133], ref [232]. In this setting, optimal sensor placement should be judged not only by nominal information gain, but also by its ability to reduce posterior uncertainty in damage-sensitive parameters and maintain acceptable probability of detection under uncertain conditions ref [233], ref [234].

Recent work points toward integrating UQ with optimization through Bayesian experimental design, sparse sensing, and stochastic model updating. Information-theoretic criteria such as expected utility and entropy reduction provide a principled route for selecting sensor layouts under uncertainty ref [57], while Bayesian finite-element updating offers a framework for propagating uncertainty from model class and data to posterior structural parameters ref [235]. For damage diagnosis, probabilistic formulations based on Gaussian-process surrogates and hierarchical Bayesian learning can substantially reduce computational burden while preserving uncertainty estimates, which is crucial for large-scale infrastructure applications ref [236], ref [237].

Open challenges remain in calibrating aleatory versus epistemic uncertainty, handling distribution shift caused by changing environmental and operational conditions, and translating posterior uncertainty into risk-based maintenance actions. Future research should couple reliability methods such as subset simulation and rare-event estimation with SHM decision pipelines ref [238], and embed robust or reliability-based optimization directly into sensor placement and monitoring policy design. Progress will also depend on benchmark studies that compare UQ methods using calibrated probabilistic metrics rather than point-estimate accuracy alone.

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Open Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
A persistent barrier to cumulative progress in structural health monitoring (SHM) and sensor placement optimization is the lack of widely accepted benchmark datasets, common damage taxonomies, and standardized evaluation protocols. Much of the literature still relies on laboratory-specific setups, proprietary finite-element models, or simulated disturbances, making cross-study comparison difficult and often obscuring whether gains arise from optimization strategy, sensing assumptions, or problem formulation. Community use of shared experimental baselines such as the IASC-ASCE benchmark structure and large civil infrastructure monitoring programs has shown the value of common testbeds for comparing identification, damage detection, and feature-selection methods under realistic environmental and operational variability ref [239], ref [240], ref [156].

Benchmarking should move beyond raw detection accuracy to include metrics directly relevant to optimization in SHM: robustness to environmental and operational variability, sensitivity to modeling error, computational cost, observability/identifiability, communication burden, and life-cycle value of information. Existing public datasets from long-term bridge and building monitoring, including the Z24 Bridge, the Alamosa Canyon Bridge, and the Tianjin Yonghe Bridge, provide important precedents because they capture temperature, traffic, and long-duration operational effects that challenge idealized placement and inference methods ref [241], ref [242], ref [243]. Likewise, the Los Alamos National Laboratory studies on data normalization and damage-sensitive feature validation underscore the need for benchmark protocols that separate environmental compensation from true damage inference ref [244], ref [245].

Future benchmarking frameworks should therefore couple open datasets with reproducible optimization pipelines, standardized train/validation/test splits across damage scenarios, uncertainty-aware scoring rules, and transparent reporting of sensor budget constraints. Shared simulation environments, such as the benchmark studies for statistical pattern recognition and vibration-based damage identification, can complement field data when used with clearly documented assumptions and domain-shift tests ref [239], ref [244], ref [246]. Progress toward community-wide repositories and objective comparison standards will be essential for translating promising optimization methods into reliable, generalizable SHM practice ref [247].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Open Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Toward Autonomous and Self-Optimizing SHM Systems
subsections.content:
A central frontier in structural health monitoring (SHM) is the transition from offline diagnosis to autonomous, closed-loop systems that can sense, interpret, and reconfigure themselves under changing operational and environmental conditions. Early visions of smart sensor networks emphasized decentralized decision making, embedded processing, and adaptive coordination, thereby laying the groundwork for self-organizing monitoring architectures suitable for resource-constrained civil infrastructure ref [248], ref [142]. More recent cyber-physical perspectives further argue that autonomy in SHM requires tight coupling among sensing, communication, model updating, and actuation rather than isolated advances in damage detection algorithms ref [249].

Self-optimizing SHM systems will likely depend on reinforcement learning, multi-agent coordination, and active sensing to decide where, when, and how to measure. Reinforcement learning has already shown promise for optimal sensor scheduling in wireless sensor networks and for adaptive control under uncertainty, offering a natural paradigm for sequential monitoring decisions with energy, bandwidth, and risk constraints ref [250], ref [251]. In parallel, active perception and informative path planning in robotics provide algorithmic templates for mobile or reconfigurable sensing platforms that seek measurements maximizing information gain while respecting operational constraints ref [252], ref [253].

However, full autonomy raises unresolved issues in safety, interpretability, and verification. Learning-enabled SHM agents must remain robust to distribution shift, sparse damage data, and communication failures, while producing decisions that are certifiable for high-consequence infrastructure. Recent work on safe reinforcement learning and trustworthy autonomy highlights the need to embed constraints, uncertainty awareness, and human oversight directly into autonomous decision loops ref [254], ref [255]. Future research should therefore focus on benchmarked closed-loop testbeds, hierarchical human-on-the-loop architectures, and digital-twin-driven policies that jointly optimize sensing, diagnosis, and intervention over the structure life cycle.
